## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the reservation agents is the natural last step before the study goes out, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: The question itself is plain, but the hint packs video, typing, a preselection, credits and text-message delivery into one block, and it says 'voice' while the video and the recorded answer speak of a face, so I would read it twice.
screens.why3: Picking which interviewer my agents will hear is my own decision as the founder, and I can make it from the two samples.
screens.why4: Two named voices with 5-second samples are distinct and enough, but my agents are in Germany and nothing says whether either one speaks German or with what accent, which is the one thing I would choose on.
screens.why5: Nothing of Codyco, the AI receptionist or the hotel director's role leaks into the interviewer choice, and it keeps 'reservation agents' as I typed it.
screens.instead: Who should ask reservation agents your questions? (both speak German; tap to hear) -- Daphne ▶ 5 s · Saskia ▶ 5 s

screens.why1: After choosing who asks the questions, choosing how the reservation agents answer is the natural last setup step before sending.
screens.why2: Plain words: video interviewer, read and tap, let them choose; each option is explained in one short line.
screens.why3: As founder I know my agents work on a busy desk or central office between calls, so I can judge whether they'd rather tap than talk on video.
screens.why4: The three options cover the real choices (voice/video, text, both) and are distinct, with no escape needed for a format choice.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles is distorted; it only sets the respondents' answering mode, and 'reservation agents' is my own actor word.

screens.why1: After choosing how agents will answer, the last step is deciding who receives the link, so the question comes at the obvious point before sending.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but the second option mentions a 'Contacts page' I have not seen anywhere in this flow, and it switches from 'I' to 'you send them', so it needs a second read.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm sending to agents I know by name, such as the 7 groups' reservation offices, or posting in a hoteliers' group, so I can answer this from my own plans.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel-found list and one open link for a group are distinct, cover the real ways I would reach reservation agents, and need no escape chip.
screens.why5: This is a pure sending-logistics screen, so nothing of my idea, numbers or roles is at stake or leaks.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name (I send each one their own link) / People I find with Keel's contact search (I pick a list, Keel makes a link for each, I send them) / A group, with one open link (I post it where they already are; each person signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits under the title, and the tally beside it gives the deciding number: 4 beliefs, 4 holding, 7 people answered.
screens.why_b2: Each card's line says what was counted, over how many and where my bar sits ('7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7'), though the Importance line is printed twice.
screens.why_b3: Prevalence, Frequency and Current solution are my beliefs as I checked them. The Importance line repeats my whole circumstance and 'five things that are hard' before it gets to the point, so I recognise it but would not have said it that way.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what four holding beliefs mean for Codyco or what I should do next; the only explainer is how the verdict is computed.
screens.why_b5: Every card shows the 7, but nothing says 7 is a small sample, and the 5% and seven-figure loss in my statement sit under 'Holding up' as if the study had tested them, when it only asked whether calls ring out and how often.
screens.instead: Holding up with 7 reservation agents: every belief cleared its bar, and calls ringing out is a near-daily problem. But 7 is few, and the 5% and the seven-figure loss were not tested here, so go next to whether directors will pay €3,000 for the pilot.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside '7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7', so I can see it held and by how much against my 'at least 8 in 10'.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 7 cells all for me on a 0-to-7 axis with my bar marked at 6, so what is counted, out of how many and where my bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: I recognise it, but the belief line drops my segment ('at hotel groups in Germany that run a central reservations office or call center'), and 'let a guest's booking call ring out' puts the blame on the agent where I wrote 'not every one gets answered'; the stray '— the most recent time it happened' after the question also muddies what was asked.
screens.why_b4: 'How often, and whether it matters, are the next two cards' tells me where to look next, but not what a 7-of-7 result means for selling Codyco to hotel groups.
screens.why_b5: n is visible, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and 'Common among these 7' claims nothing beyond the people who answered.
screens.instead: At least 8 in 10 reservation agents at German hotel groups with a central office or call center had a booking call go unanswered in the last 7 days: holding up, 7 of 7 said yes against your bar of 6 of 7, a lean from a small group; missed calls look near-universal, so next check whether they happen often enough and cost enough to pay €3,000 to fix.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 inside my 5 to 7 days and a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: The count and the bar marker at 5 are plain, but the legend's 'what you said' and 'at what you said' need a second look, and the 0 tick suggests an answer nobody could give.
screens.why_b3: Frequency, with 'let a guest's booking call ring out on 5 to 7 days out of 7', is my range in a reservation desk's own words, though the Asked line's tail 'the most recent time it happened' does not fit a count over 7 days.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' only sends me on and does not say what missed calls on 6 days in 7 mean for the pilot I am selling.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and called 'a lean, not a call', and nothing claims more than 6 of 7 agents.
screens.instead: Missed booking calls come up on most shifts (6 of 7 agents, middle answer 6 days), so a missed-call pilot has work every week; whether agents care enough is the next card.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits beside 6 of 7 put it in their two against a bar of 5 of 7, so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together, though the count is printed twice in a row.
screens.why_b2: The caption tells me it counts picks, 14 from 7 people picking two each, my row is marked with 6 against 2 for each of the others, and the strip under it shows 6 for, 1 against and the marker at 5.
screens.why_b3: Importance and my missed-call row, Answering booking calls before they ring out, sit at the top of the card against the five things I listed, though the question's 'your last guest call' is not quite my 'shift with a missed call'.
screens.why_b4: The So line explains what the count means (top two, not first) but not what to do with the idea: whether to lead with missed calls, or what Chiara's group-email answer says about groups whose call center already covers the evening.
screens.why_b5: It keeps n at 7, calls this a small group (a lean, not a call), and its So line refuses to claim the problem ranks first.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 agents put missed booking calls in their top two. Lead with it. The one against (Chiara) has a call center covering evenings and is losing time to group emails, so check how many of your groups already cover after hours before you price.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits beside the deciding count, '7 of 7 said today's way falls short', and the 'bar 5 of 7', so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts each person's last missed call on my five rungs, over 7 people, with my line drawn under 'All called back that day' and the strip's marker at 5. All three are plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Current solution and grades my own rungs word for word, from 'Every missed call called back within the hour' down to 'Calls that rang out were simply lost', so the belief about getting back to a call that rang out is mine.
screens.why_b4: 'Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study' is close to a generic line. It does not say that 5 of 7 call back only 'when there was time', which tells me to pitch an answer in the moment rather than a faster callback.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the screen says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and 7 of 7 is reported as counted, not called strong or proven.
screens.instead: Today's way falls short for all 7 of these 7, but mostly as slow callbacks: 5 of 7 called back only when there was time. Lead the next study on answering the call as it rings, not on calling back faster.

screens.why_b1: The status word Holding up sits beside its deciding number, 6 of 7 put it in their two against a bar of 5 of 7, and the line Importance held, 6 of 7 ties them together.
screens.why_b3: The dimension is Importance and the belief line is the one I checked, with my five hard things, my circumstance and answering booking calls before they ring out.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what the one dissent means for Codyco, for example that groups whose call center already covers after six are a weaker first target or that the pitch should change for them.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 and the single dissent are plain, and nothing is generalised beyond the one person who said no.
screens.why_b6: Chiara's quote tells me something I did not write: where a call center already covers the evening, the pain moves to group emails without rates, which marks a segment where my missed-call pitch lands weaker.
screens.instead: Add one line under the quote: 'The one who put it outside their two has a call center covering after six; groups that already have after-hours cover may not feel the missed calls, so lead with peak and holiday gaps, or qualify on after-hours cover first.'

screens.why1: As the first screen it checks whether I work in a hotel group's central reservations office, which is plainly the gate for a study about booking calls.
screens.why2: Central reservations office and call centre are the words of my trade, so I know at once it means my Zentralreservierung in Munich.
screens.why3: I take booking calls in our central office every shift, so I can answer this without thinking.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it completely for a screener, and the gate needs no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment of German hotel groups running a central reservations office or call centre, and nothing about a product reaches me.
screens.why6: The question itself is one breath, but 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' is clumsy for a yes-or-no, where the guidelines say a screener ends with just 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: Do you take booking calls for a German hotel group's central reservations office? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I take calls for a central reservations office, asking whether a booking call went unanswered is the obvious next thing to check.
screens.why2: Ring out is clear enough, but on our floor we would say a call dropped out of the queue or went unanswered, and let makes it sound like I chose to ignore it.
screens.why3: On a trade-fair Saturday the system queues calls and I am on another guest, so I often don't see which calls rang out unless I check the queue board; I would partly be guessing.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and the chips belong to the story box, not to this question.
screens.why5: It still asks about booking calls that don't get answered, and nothing of anyone's product or plan reaches me.
screens.why6: One short sentence followed by Yes or no is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: The gate names the window and the costly event rather than the routine of taking calls: an agent whose every call was picked up truly says No, and one who missed a call says Yes, so the belief can go either way.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a guest's booking call to you go unanswered? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after I said yes to letting a booking call ring out this week, it makes sense to ask on how many days it happened.
screens.why2: I understand 'ring out', but in our office we'd say a call was missed or dropped out of the queue, and 'you let' makes it sound like I chose to ignore it.
screens.why3: On a fair Saturday the calls queue up while I'm on another line, so I see missed calls on the board but can't always say they were mine; I would partly guess.
screens.why4: One button per day from 1 to 7 with 'I can't recall' apart covers every answer, even though I only worked about five of those days.
screens.why5: It still asks about booking calls that went unanswered, and nothing about a product or the company's plan reaches me.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, and 'say a number from 1 to 7, or say you can't recall' is easy to hold on the phone.
screens.why7: The options are on the one measure, days of the window, from 1 to 7 with no zero and the one escape apart; the event is an act on a given day, and the founder's low can split the buttons.
screens.instead: On how many of the last 7 days did a booking call to you go unanswered? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 7 · I can't recall

screens.why1: After two screens on letting booking calls ring out, asking which part of my phone work I'd most like made easier follows naturally on the third screen.
screens.why2: Changes to bookings, group requests, quoting the rate while the guest waits and calls that ring out are all everyday words in our office; I get it on first reading.
screens.why3: I do every one of these on a Saturday shift in the central office, so I can pick from my own day without guessing.
screens.why4: Group requests that come by email are a different channel from the guest call I'm told to think of, so that one sits oddly; the others are distinct and in my words.
screens.why5: Answering booking calls before they ring out says exactly the problem the earlier screens asked about, and nothing of a product or plan reaches me.
screens.why6: One short question and five short parallel phrases I can hold, then one escape, said cleanly with no slash or bracket.
screens.why7: The own item is there, not first, and there are four rivals, so a pick can go for or against, with None of these as the one escape; but the email rival drifts to another channel, which the card rules out for a row.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Handling changes to existing bookings; answering guests' questions about their stay; finding a room when the city is nearly full; quoting the right rate while the guest waits; or answering booking calls before they ring out. Or say none of these.

screens.why1: Right after I said calls rang out on me this week, asking what happened with getting back to those callers is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: The question asks about one call that rang out, but the answers talk about every, all, some and few calls, so I have to read it twice to know if they mean my last missed call or the whole week.
screens.why3: I know whether we rang the missed numbers back from the callback list on a trade-fair Saturday, and roughly when.
screens.why4: The answers mix how fast we called back with how many we called back, so 'some called back when there was time' and 'few were ever called back' do not line up with 'within the hour' and 'that day', and nothing fits a single call that we rang back the next morning.
screens.why5: 'Rang out', 'called back' and 'booking call' are how we talk at the desk, and nothing about anyone's product reaches me.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is one short question and five short answers I can hold, then the single escape at the end.
screens.why7: The first rung works and the last fails, and the escape fits a callback that could be handed off, but the measure is bent: rungs one and two grade speed while three and four grade share, and the last rung, 'Calls that rang out were simply lost', is the card's own named example of an outcome standing in for the measure.
screens.instead: Think of the last booking call that rang out. When was the guest called back? Within the hour · Later the same day · The next day · Days later · Never called back · Someone else did it
